newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ phones companies told to act on portability.
newsitem.headline: NZ phones companies told to act on portability.

text.p: Phone companies need to make faster progress on interconnection agreements for new players and number portability or risk government intervention, Communications Minister Maurice Williamson said on Wednesday.

Williamson, addressing a conference of telecommunications users in Wellington, said the government did not want to have to regulate the industry but was growing tired of threatening the majors players -- Telecom NZ, Clear, BellSouth and others -- "over and over again".
"If you can't fix this yourselves and if you can't negotiate through this in a commercially sensible manner, then you will give me no option," Williamson said.
Number portability -- the ability of a phone user to retain his or her phone number when changing carrier -- is considered necessary if competitive phone services are really to develop.
The industry has been haggling over the issue for months and Williamson criticised Telecom's role in the process.
"Telecom's initial pricing offer for number portability could be said to have been totally out of anybody's ballpark," he said.
"To its credit it came back, nearly six months later, with a more realistic offer.
"Telecom obviously stands to gain in delays to the introduction of portability...There's always a nagging feeling that more progress could be made."
Williamson said he expected owners of natural communication monopolies to provide interconnection on terms that promoted efficiencies and delivered benefits to consumers.

The Government was keen to consider any proposals had to be sure a net benefit would result. It was not interested in merely "shifting profits from one carrier to another without seeing real user benefits."
"I will make it plain that other carriers' conduct in negotiations does not always stand up to scrutiny either.

"BellSouth and Clear in particular also have incentives to exaggerate the difficulty of concluding deals. They have incentives to enlist public support and seek regulatory changes to advance their own interests."

Williamson said that he had been deluged by complaints in recent weeks on numbering and number portability issues "most of which I consider could be quickly resolved if all concerned took a more realistic position."
Some of the issues raised had little or no substance and were accompanied by demands for heavy-handed regulatory intervention to resolve them.
The minister urged all concerned to take a fresh look at their approach to interconnection matters.
He went on to warn all players that "should it be necessary for Government to become involved you could all loose out in some degree".
"Some other parties would prefer to retain their share of the cake than fight for it in the marketplace," he said.
"The Government's overriding concern is to increase the size of the cake, especially for users,'' not with any particular operators share of the cake, he added.
